# Sync and async, side by side

![](../images/spot-1.svg){.spot fig-alt="A small isometric town on a yellow tile, joined to a blue-topped Postgres cylinder by two pipes; an elephant in a hoodie works on a laptop in front."}
SQLAlchemy 2.0 runs the same statements, the same models and the same results in two styles. In
sync code each call blocks until the database answers. In async code the call is `await`ed, and the
process can do other work while it waits. Learning to write either takes an afternoon. This chapter
is about what async buys, and where it bites.

## One driver, two engines

SQLAlchemy picks the database driver from the URL. psycopg 3 implements both the blocking and the
asyncio interfaces, so one `DATABASE_URL` can serve a sync engine for scripts and migrations and an
async engine for the web app:

```python
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine

url = "postgresql+psycopg://app:pwd@localhost:5432/app"
engine = create_engine(url)              # scripts, Alembic, pandas
async_engine = create_async_engine(url)  # FastAPI
```

With `postgresql+asyncpg://` only the async engine would work, and with `psycopg2` only the sync
one. That is why the lab uses psycopg by default.

Most of the code is the same in both styles. The table lists what differs:

| | sync | async |
|---|---|---|
| engine | `create_engine(url)` | `create_async_engine(url)` |
| connection and transaction | `with engine.connect()` / `engine.begin()` | `async with engine.connect()` / `engine.begin()` |
| session | `Session(engine)`, `sessionmaker` | `AsyncSession(engine)`, `async_sessionmaker` |
| a round trip to the database | a plain call | `await` |
| `select`, `insert`, `text`, models | identical | identical |
| lazy loading | works | raises |

Only the round trip is awaited. `await conn.execute(...)` fetches the rows, and reading them with
`.one()`, `.all()` or `.scalars()` afterwards is in-memory work with no `await`.

## The lazy-loading trap

A lazy load is a query that SQLAlchemy fires when you touch a relationship attribute that has not
been loaded yet. In `author.notes` there is nowhere to put an `await`. Rather than block the event
loop, the async session raises an error:

```python
author = (await session.execute(select(Author))).scalars().first()
author.notes   # MissingGreenlet: greenlet_spawn has not been called
```

The same happens to attributes that `commit()` has expired, which is why `AsyncSession` is almost
always created with `expire_on_commit=False`. There are three ways out, best first. Eager-load what
you need with `selectinload(Author.notes)`. Load it explicitly with
`await session.refresh(author, ["notes"])`. Or add `AsyncAttrs` to the model and write
`await author.awaitable_attrs.notes`.

## What async buys: overlapping waits

A single query is not faster async. What changes is what the process does while the database is
busy. Ten queries that each spend 200 ms on the server take about 2 s one after another. Under
`asyncio.gather`, with a pooled connection for each, they take about 200 ms. A thread pool gets the
same overlap, at the price of one thread per query.

The connection pool sets the ceiling. `create_async_engine` defaults to `pool_size=5` and
`max_overflow=10`, so 15 queries can overlap and the 16th waits for a free connection. In every case
the database does the same total work, and only the client stops idling. If the bottleneck is the
database's CPU, async changes nothing.

## Watching it happen

The lab's app answers questions about the SQLAlchemy documentation with pgvector. Its `POST /trace`
endpoint answers the same questions twice with tracing on. The **sync** run takes them one after
another on one connection. The **async** run gives each question its own task and connection under
`gather`. The scene below replays one such pair on a shared clock.

::: {.viz .scene .column-body-outset data-src="../viz/index.html?embed=1" data-poster="../images/city.gif" data-title="Vector search with pgvector, sync and async"}
:::
::: {.viz-caption .column-body-outset}
Six questions, sync on the left and async on the right. Each question drops into Python (embedding
with `bge-small`), crosses to its Postgres backend, and lights its five matching chunks in the
documentation field as the HNSW walk returns. Run it live to orbit the scene, or press Replay inside it.
[Open full screen](../viz/index.html){target="_blank"}.
:::

The async plate finishes while the sync one is still working through its queue, and the two wall
times in the corner show by how much. Each backend on the async plate is a separate Postgres
process, because Postgres starts one process per connection. That is the cost of the trade:
concurrency on the client is paid for in connections on the server, and [PgBouncer](pgbouncer.qmd)
exists to manage that cost.

## Sync code from async code

pandas, Alembic and much older code want a sync connection. Inside async code, `run_sync` hands
them one that is bridged onto the async connection, so a second engine is not needed:

```python
async with async_engine.connect() as conn:
    df = await conn.run_sync(lambda c: pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM events", c))
```

## Which one to use

- **Scripts, notebooks, batch jobs and migrations**: sync. Every library works, and stack traces
  are simpler.
- **Web services, and anything that waits on many databases or APIs at once**: async, with eager
  loading, `expire_on_commit=False`, and a pool sized for your concurrency.
- **A mixed code base**: one driver (psycopg 3), one URL, both engines, and `run_sync` where the two
  meet.

::: {.callout-note}
